Idioms.phrase: Charley horse - A cramp or stiff leg.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Billy had to stop running because of a terrible charley horse.

Idioms.phrase: Charmed life - A life that seems extraordinarily lucky and strangely free of unpleasant consequences.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Elizabeth seemed to live a charmed life. No matter how many stupid things she did, everything always seemed to turn out okay.

Idioms.phrase: Chasing rainbows - Trying to pursue unrealistic dreams.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Monica thinks that she will become a famous actress one day, but I think she's just chasing rainbows.

Idioms.phrase: Checkered past - A questionable past with many questionable actions, especially frowned upon or criminal activities.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Maxwell had a checkered past. It seemed that he had a criminal record and there were many strange rumors about him.

Idioms.phrase: Cheer up - To feel happier when you're sad.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Cheer up! You look so sad. What's wrong?

Idioms.phrase: Chew someone out - To scold someone.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Jane was angry with her friend for betraying her. She definitely chewed her out.

Idioms.phrase: Chew something over - To thoroughly think or talk about something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I spent a long time chewing it over before I made a final decision. I always think things through like that.

Idioms.phrase: Chewing the fat - Talking about something, usually just chatting.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The two best friends enjoyed chewing the fat as much as they could. They loved nothing more than an afternoon of good conversation.

Idioms.phrase: Chow down - Eat heartily.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, This pizza looks delicious. Let's chow down!

Idioms.phrase: Chuffed to bits - Very pleased or happy.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I was chuffed to bits about my birthday presents! They were all so nice.

Idioms.phrase: Clean slate - A fresh beginning.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Wouldn't it be nice to start over again with a clean slate? I'd love to be free of regrets and worries.

Idioms.phrase: Clean someone out - To steal or take all of a person's possessions and/or money.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The property was recently robbed. The thieves completely cleaned the owners out of all their money and equipment.

Idioms.phrase: Clear as mud - Not clear at all and therefore difficult to understand.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I really wanted to play the new board game, but I found the instructions to be as clear as mud. It was really confusing.

Idioms.phrase: Clear the air - To resolve a disagreement or address and resolve a resentment.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, We decided to clear the air with Maria. We knew that she resented some of the things that we had done and so we talked to her and apologized.

Idioms.phrase: Climb the walls - To feel restless.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, They felt closed in that winter. It was really cold outside, and they were climbing the walls, wishing it was spring and that they could go outside and play some sports.

Idioms.phrase: Close but no cigar - Closely approaching success or the right answer, but not quite there.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, During the quiz show, Joseph gave his answer to the first question, certain he had it right. But he was wrong, so the host said "close but no cigar."

Idioms.phrase: Close shave - Just managing to escape.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, We managed to free ourselves from the situation but it was a close shave. We almost weren't able to.

Idioms.phrase: Closed-minded - To be unable or unwilling to listen to and think about new ideas or perspectives.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I didn't like William. I found him very closed-minded. He refused to listen to any ideas that contradicted anything he already thought.

Idioms.phrase: Clown around - To joke around, telling jokes and being silly.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The teacher got frustrated with her students. They wouldn't stop clowning around and they refused to concentrate on the work at hand.

Idioms.phrase: Cock-and-bull story - An implausible or far-fetched story.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Yes, Corey told me about his adventures in Europe. I think it's a cock-and-bull story.

Idioms.phrase: Coin a new term - To come up with a new way of saying something (a word or phrase) .
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Meredith is quite creative. She actually coined a new term yesterday. I joked that maybe it should be added to the dictionary!

Idioms.phrase: Coin a phrase - To invent a new phrase or way of expressing something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I ended up coining a new phrase yesterday. People said they'd never heard something described that way before.

Idioms.phrase: Cold enough to freeze the ball off a brass monkey - Very cold.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I was so cold yesterday, even with a heavy coat on. It was cold enough to freeze the balls off a brass monkey.

Idioms.phrase: Cold feet - To feel nervous to the point of thinking about removing yourself from a situation.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Ethan had cold feet about the speech. Even though he had practiced it, he got so nervous beforehand that he felt like running away.

Idioms.phrase: Cold shoulder - To be cold and unfriendly to someone.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Mia gave me the cold shoulder the other day; she acted as if she barely knew me.

Idioms.phrase: Collecting dust - Not being used.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The vase had been collecting dust on that table for many years. They just never used it.

Idioms.phrase: Come a long way - To progress in some area in life.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I feel that I've come a long way from how I was a few years ago. I'm much more successful now.

Idioms.phrase: Come alive - To gain animation in some way.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, All of the ideas in the book came alive when I saw the documentary.

Idioms.phrase: Come clean - To tell the truth about something that one has done wrong.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The police officer advised the person she arrested to come clean with what he had done. It was better to just tell the truth, she said.

Idioms.phrase: Come clean - To tell the truth about something that one has done wrong.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The police officer advised the person she arrested to come clean with what he had done. It was better to just tell the truth, she said.

Idioms.phrase: Come down with a cold - To show symptoms of a cold.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I came down with a cold after going for a long hike in intemperate weather.

Idioms.phrase: Come hell or high water - No matter what.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, We're going to Mexico this year, come hell or high water. Nothing will stop us!

Idioms.phrase: Come in handy - To end up being useful.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, That tool ended up coming in handy after I’d had it for a while.

Idioms.phrase: Come out of your shell - To stop being so shy.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, We all hoped that Helen would come out of her shell soon. She was shy and got so nervous around new people.

Idioms.phrase: Come out smelling like roses/a rose - To come out seeming like a wonderful person, especially when it's not fair.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, We were all very frustrated. Even though Patricia had done all sorts of bad things, she always came out smelling like a rose. People thought she was wonderful.

Idioms.phrase: Come rain or shine - Something will be accomplished no matter what.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Ryan said that he would definitely get the job done, come rain or shine.

Idioms.phrase: Comfort food - Food that comforts you and makes you feel better.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, What is your favorite comfort food? I think mine is macaroni and cheese, or maybe hot chicken soup.

Idioms.phrase: Comparing apples to oranges - Comparing two entirely different things that really should not, or cannot, be compared.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Mary asked Veronica which pair of pants she liked best, but Veronica said that the styles were so different that it would be like comparing apples to oranges.

Idioms.phrase: Computer crashed - Computer is no longer working.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Darryl's computer crashed yesterday. He's in a panic, trying to figure out what to do to fix it.

Idioms.phrase: Cook someone's goose - To ruin their plans.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, It turned out that their goose was cooked. Their plan was ruined.

Idioms.phrase: Cook up - To plan or invent.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, They were highly skilled at cooking up new ideas that the boss loved. We wished that we could be that inventive.

Idioms.phrase: Cooked the books - To do bookkeeping or accounting in a dishonest way, often to avoid taxes.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The company was a shady one. Lots of people said that they cooked the books.

Idioms.phrase: Cool as a cucumber - Calm and relaxed.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Jim never gets worried about interviews. He always seems to be cool as a cucumber.

Idioms.phrase: Cool your jets - Calm down.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, There's no need to get so angry about this! Cool your jets.

Idioms.phrase: Copycat - Someone who copies something someone else has done.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, One of the kids in class said that the boy beside him was a copycat because he copied some of his math homework.

Idioms.phrase: Cost me a mint - It cost me a lot of money.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The luxury car cost him a mint! It was extremely expensive.

Idioms.phrase: Costs an arm and a leg - Costs a lot of money.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, They were thinking about buying a boat but decided not to. The problem was that it cost an arm and a leg.

Idioms.phrase: Couch potato - Someone who spends a lot of time on the couch in front of the TV.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, They are worried about their cousin's health because he is such a couch potato. He doesn't get enough exercise.

Idioms.phrase: Couldn't care less - Expresses complete lack of interest in something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Honestly, I couldn't care less about not being invited to the party. It just doesn't matter to me.

Idioms.phrase: Country mile - A long distance.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, It turned out we had to walk a country mile to get to Annie's house. It took forever.

Idioms.phrase: Cover a lot of ground - Get a lot of things done, in a variety of areas.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, We expect to cover a lot of ground during our meeting today. There are lots of things that we need to discuss.

Idioms.phrase: Crack a book - To open a book and read it.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Why are you so surprised that you don't know very much about anything? You need to crack a book sometimes.

Idioms.phrase: Crack open a cold one - Open a cold can of beer.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, After a long day at work, they decided to crack open a cold one and sit outside on the porch for a while.

Idioms.phrase: Crack someone up - Make someone laugh.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I love that comedian. She always cracks me up!

Idioms.phrase: Crank out a paper - To write a paper (or essay) in a mechanical sort of way, probably in a rush.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The students cranked out the paper that was due the next day.

Idioms.phrase: Cream of the crop - The best.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, These students were the cream of the crop in their class. They had extremely impressive grades.

Idioms.phrase: Crickets - Complete silence or lack of communication about something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I called Sarah the other day and left a message asking if she'd like to come over for dinner. The response: crickets!

Idioms.phrase: Crocodile tears - Fake tears.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Noah started to cry about the situation, but we knew it was just crocodile tears.

Idioms.phrase: Cross that bridge when you come to it - Deal with the problem when it becomes an obstacle.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Isabella tended to be a worrier, letting things overwhelm her mind. There was one potential problem that was making her very anxious. Her best friend told her to cross that bridge when she came to it.

Idioms.phrase: Cross your fingers - Hope that my wish comes true.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I'm hoping I'll win that prize in the raffle. Cross your fingers for me.

Idioms.phrase: Crunch time - A time when things need to finally get done.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, It's crunch time at work. We've got lots of deadlines coming up and there's lots of work to do.

Idioms.phrase: Cup of Joe - Cup of coffee.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Adam always started his day with a cup of Joe. He didn't think he could function without coffee!

Idioms.phrase: Curiosity killed the cat - It can be dangerous to be too curious and ask too many questions.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, If I were you, I wouldn't ask any more questions. Remember: curiosity killed the cat.

Idioms.phrase: Curve ball - Something that is deceptive or confusing.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, His boss threw him a real curve ball the other day. He wanted him to restart the entire project.

Idioms.phrase: Cut and dried - Unequivocal or clear, or perhaps routine.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The instructions were cut and dried—they left no room for questions.

Idioms.phrase: Cut someone off at the knees - To humiliate someone or compel them to do something you want.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Daniel felt his supervisor was cutting him off at the knees by the way he was criticizing his work.

Idioms.phrase: Cut the mustard - Do something well or up to standard.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Chloe tried her best in completing the task, but people said that she just didn't cut the mustard.

Idioms.phrase: Cut them some slack - Refrain from being too critical of someone.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, He did poorly on the test but studied hard. Cut him some slack!

Idioms.phrase: Cut to the chase - Get to the point quickly.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, We only have about fifteen minutes for this meeting, so I'm going to have to cut to the chase.

Idioms.phrase: Cut to the quick - To deeply wound or hurt someone.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Amy felt cut to the quick when her friends rejected her. She cried for a long time afterward.
